md: A **monomer** is a small molecule that can join to others like it; a **polymer** is the very long chain molecule made when thousands of them join. The process is **addition polymerisation**: *addition* because the monomers add on to one another and nothing else forms, *polymerisation* because a polymer results. The name is the same whatever the monomer, and each word earns a mark.

**Monomer, and not a monomer.** Fluoroethene, $\ce{CH2=CHF}$, is a monomer: its C=C lets it join on. Fluoroethane, $\ce{CH3CH2F}$, looks almost the same but is not one: every bond is single, so it has nothing to join with. A monomer for this process always has a C=C.

stem: Fluoroethene, $\ce{CH2=CHF}$, forms a polymer, and no other product is made. Name the process. **[2]**

steps.working: The monomers add on to one another, and nothing else forms: **addition**.
steps.decision: Addition is the first word and the first mark: it says how they join, with no second product.

steps.working: One very long chain molecule, a polymer, is made: **polymerisation**.
steps.decision: Polymerisation is the second word and the second mark. Written on its own it earns only one of the two.

title: Before you watch
md: This clip is made for a separate Chemistry course: condensation polymers, natural polymers and recycling are not on your specification.

title: GCSE Chemistry Revision "Addition Polymers" (Triple)
why: Monomers joining into a polymer, shown step by step.

prompt: Asked to name the process in which dichloroethene molecules join into a polymer, a student writes only: polymerisation. What does the answer lose?
options: the mark for addition: the name has two words, and each earns a mark
nothing: polymerisation is the full name
both marks: polymerisation is the name of a different process
answer: the mark for addition: the name has two words, and each earns a mark
explain: Steps 1 and 2 of See it earn one mark each: addition says the monomers add on with nothing else formed, and polymerisation says a polymer is made. Polymerisation on its own is half the name, so it keeps one mark and loses the other.

optionNotes.option: nothing: polymerisation is the full name
optionNotes.why: Polymerisation says a polymer forms but not how, and the scheme gives a separate mark for the word addition.

optionNotes.option: both marks: polymerisation is the name of a different process
optionNotes.why: Polymerisation is the right word, so it keeps its own mark; only the missing word addition costs one.

twin.prompt: Which word of the name addition polymerisation says that no other product is formed?
options: addition
polymerisation
monomer
twin.explain: Addition says the monomers simply add on to one another, so nothing else is made: step 1 of See it. Polymerisation only says that a polymer is the result.

optionNotes.option: polymerisation
optionNotes.why: Polymerisation says what is made, a polymer, not whether anything else is made with it.

optionNotes.option: monomer
optionNotes.why: Monomer is not part of the process's name at all; it is the small molecule that joins up.

md: When one bond of a C=C opens, each of its two carbons gains a spare bond, and that spare bond links it to the next monomer. Only one of the two bonds opens, so the carbons of each monomer stay joined, now by a single bond. Nothing leaves: the chain holds every atom the monomers brought.

title: Why nothing else is made
md: No atom leaves when a bond opens, so no second product forms. Section 7 turns this into a check on every repeat unit you draw.

stem: Three ethene molecules, $\ce{C2H4}$, join into a section of chain, as the picture at the top shows. Say what happens to the bonds, and count the atoms in the chain.

steps.working: One bond of each C=C opens, which leaves each carbon one spare bond.
steps.decision: Only one of the two bonds opens: the two carbons of each monomer stay joined.

steps.working: The spare bonds link the monomers: $3 \times 2 = 6$ carbons in a row, every bond between them single.
steps.decision: Each monomer brings its two carbons, so the chain grows two carbons at a time.

steps.working: Nothing leaves: $3 \times 4 = 12$ hydrogens, the same as in the three ethene molecules.
steps.decision: Counting the atoms before and after checks that nothing was lost.

prompt: Fluoroethene molecules join into a chain in the same way. How are the chain's carbon atoms joined to each other?
options: by single bonds
by double bonds
they are not joined at all
explain: Step 1 of See it: only one bond of each C=C opens, and the freed bond links the carbon to the next molecule, so every bond along the chain is one line. A carbon that kept its double bond and linked on as well would have five bonds.

optionNotes.option: by double bonds
optionNotes.why: The monomer had a double bond, so it is easy to think the chain keeps it, but one of its two bonds is what opened to link on.

optionNotes.option: they are not joined at all
optionNotes.why: Only one of the two bonds opens, so the carbons of each monomer stay joined, and the freed bonds join them to their neighbours too.

twin.prompt: In the chain, how many bonds does each carbon atom make in all?
options: four
three
five
twin.explain: Carbon always makes four bonds. A chain carbon has two to its neighbours in the chain and two to the groups it carries, which is why the bonds between chain carbons must be single.

optionNotes.option: three
optionNotes.why: Three counts only the two chain bonds and one group, but every chain carbon also carries a second group.

optionNotes.option: five
optionNotes.why: Five would mean the double bond was kept as well as the new link, and carbon never makes more than four bonds.

text: 3. Why an alkane cannot join up

md: An **alkane** has only single bonds, and every one is already in use joining carbon to carbon or carbon to hydrogen. With no bond to open, no carbon gains a spare bond, so an alkane **cannot** form an addition polymer. That is why every monomer here is an **alkene**, or has a C=C like one.

stem: Hex-1-ene, $\ce{CH2=CHCH2CH2CH2CH3}$, can form an addition polymer, but hexane, $\ce{C6H14}$, cannot. Explain why. **[2]**

steps.working: Hex-1-ene has a C=C, and one of its two bonds can open to link to the next molecule.
steps.decision: The first mark is the double bond and what it does: one bond opens, freeing a bond on each carbon.

steps.working: Hexane has only single bonds, all in use, so it has no bond to open.
steps.decision: The second mark is the other half: say what the alkane lacks, not only what the alkene has.

prompt: Ethene and ethane both have two carbon atoms. Why can ethene form an addition polymer when ethane cannot?
options: ethene has a C=C, and one of its two bonds can open to link to the next molecule
ethene has more hydrogen atoms to give away
ethane molecules are too large to join together
answer: ethene has a C=C, and one of its two bonds can open to link to the next molecule
explain: Compare them as steps 1 and 2 of See it compared hex-1-ene with hexane: ethene's carbons share two bonds, and opening one frees a bond on each carbon to link on. Ethane's bonds are all single and all in use. So the reason is the C=C that can open.

optionNotes.option: ethene has more hydrogen atoms to give away
optionNotes.why: Ethene has fewer hydrogens than ethane, not more, and no hydrogen leaves when the chain forms: the joining is done by the C=C.

optionNotes.option: ethane molecules are too large to join together
optionNotes.why: Both molecules have two carbons, so size is not the difference; ethane simply has no bond to open.

twin.prompt: Pent-2-ene can form an addition polymer, but pentane cannot. Why?
options: pent-2-ene has a C=C that can open to link to the next molecule; pentane has only single bonds
pentane has more hydrogen atoms to give away
pent-2-ene molecules are smaller than pentane molecules
twin.answer: pent-2-ene has a C=C that can open to link to the next molecule; pentane has only single bonds
twin.explain: The same two halves as See it: the alkene's C=C has a bond to open, and the alkane has none, because every bond is single and in use.

optionNotes.option: pentane has more hydrogen atoms to give away
optionNotes.why: No hydrogen leaves in addition polymerisation, so a spare hydrogen is no help; what joins the chain is the C=C.

optionNotes.option: pent-2-ene molecules are smaller than pentane molecules
optionNotes.why: Both have five carbons, so size is not the difference; only the alkene has a bond it can open.

text: 4. Naming a polymer from its monomer

md: Build the polymer's name from the monomer's: **poly**, then the monomer's name **in brackets**. Ethene gives **poly(ethene)**, also called polythene; chloroethene, sold as **PVC** for window frames and drainpipes, gives **poly(chloroethene)**. Asked to name a polymer, write the chemical name, not the trade name. Read backwards, the monomer is the name inside the brackets.

title: One rule, one mark
md: Summer 2025's C2 Foundation report: most could not name the polymer made from ethene, and many left it blank. It is a rule to learn.

stem: Name the polymer made from fluoroethene, $\ce{CH2=CHF}$. **[1]**

steps.working: The monomer's name, fluoroethene, goes inside the brackets.
steps.decision: The name comes from the monomer, never from what the chain looks like, so it never ends in -ethane.

steps.working: Write poly in front: **poly(fluoroethene)**.
steps.decision: Brackets round the monomer's name; polyfluoroethene, written without them, is also accepted.

prompt: Name the polymer made from the monomer dichloroethene.
explain: The rule of step 2 of See it works for any monomer: poly, then the monomer's name in brackets, so dichloroethene gives poly(dichloroethene). The chain has only single bonds, but the name still comes from the monomer, so it never ends in -ethane.

twin.prompt: A polymer is called poly(hex-1-ene). Name the monomer it was made from.
twin.explain: Read the rule backwards: the monomer is the name inside the brackets, hex-1-ene. It has the C=C, so it could polymerise; hexane could not.

md: A polymer is too long to draw, so you draw one **repeat unit**: the part that repeats all along the chain. It shows the two carbons of the C=C joined by a **single** bond; every group each carbon had in the monomer, in the same place; a **bond through each square bracket**, because the chain carries on; and **n** after the closing bracket, because the unit repeats many times.

stem: Draw the repeat unit of poly(fluoroethene), made from $\ce{CH2=CHF}$. **[2]**

steps.working: Find the C=C: its two carbons make the chain.
steps.decision: Only the carbons of the double bond gain a spare bond when it opens.

steps.working: Join them with a single bond: F and H on the first carbon, H and H on the second.
steps.decision: Copy every group across exactly; only the bond between the carbons changes.

steps.working: Add a bond through a square bracket on each side, and n after the closing bracket.
steps.decision: The bonds through the brackets show the chain carrying on; n shows the unit repeating.

steps.working: Check: four bonds at every carbon, and $\ce{C2H3F}$, the monomer's atoms.
steps.decision: Five bonds on a carbon would mean the C=C was kept; the atom count catches a group left out.

prompt: In the repeat unit of poly(fluoroethene) drawn above, count the bonds around one carbon atom, including the bond that passes through the bracket. How many are there?
explain: Count them on the drawing, as step 4 of See it did: two to its groups, one to the other carbon and one through the bracket make four, as carbon always has. A unit that kept the double bond would give each carbon five.

twin.prompt: A student's repeat unit keeps the C=C and also has a bond through each bracket. How many bonds does each carbon then show?
twin.explain: Two to its groups, two in the double bond and one through the bracket: five. Carbon makes four, so five bonds says the double bond was kept, and the double bond is what opened.

text: 6. See it done: the structural equation

md: The structural equation shows n monomers going in and the polymer coming out: **n** in front of the monomer, drawn with its C=C, then an arrow, then the repeat unit in brackets with **n** after it. One mark is for the structure and one for n on both sides of the arrow.

steps.working: After the arrow, draw the two carbons joined by a single bond, with the F and three H where they were.
steps.decision: One bond of the C=C opens; nothing else in the molecule changes.

steps.working: Add a bond through each square bracket, and write n after the closing bracket.
steps.decision: n monomers make one chain of n units, so n appears on both sides: the second mark.

prompt: In the structural equation for fluoroethene above, which part of the drawing shows that the chain carries on beyond the repeat unit?
options: the bonds passing through the brackets
the n in front of the fluoroethene
the F atom on the first carbon
answer: the bonds passing through the brackets
explain: A bracket marks where one unit ends, and a bond crossing it says the chain does not stop there: step 3 of See it. The n counts the units; the bonds through the brackets show the chain carrying on.

optionNotes.option: the n in front of the fluoroethene
optionNotes.why: That n counts the molecules that go in; it says nothing about where the chain runs.

optionNotes.option: the F atom on the first carbon
optionNotes.why: The F is one of the groups copied from the monomer; it stays inside the brackets and shows nothing about the chain's length.

twin.prompt: In the same equation, which part shows how many fluoroethene molecules react?
options: the n in front of the monomer
the arrow
the square brackets
twin.answer: the n in front of the monomer
twin.explain: The n in front of the monomer counts the molecules that go in, step 1 of See it; the n after the bracket counts the units that come out. They are the same number, because each monomer becomes one unit.

optionNotes.option: the arrow
optionNotes.why: The arrow only says the monomers turn into the polymer; it carries no number.

optionNotes.option: the square brackets
optionNotes.why: The brackets mark off one repeat unit; the count of monomers is the n written in front of the monomer.

md:
**1.** In addition polymerisation the monomers only add on: there is no second product.
**2.** So no atom leaves the chain.
**3.** Each monomer becomes one repeat unit.
**4.** So a repeat unit has **exactly the atoms of one monomer**, only rebonded, and the same relative formula mass.

stem: Show that the repeat unit of poly(dichloroethene) has the same atoms and the same $M_r$ as dichloroethene, $\ce{CHCl=CHCl}$.

steps.working: Monomer: 2 C, 2 H and 2 Cl, so $\ce{C2H2Cl2}$.
steps.decision: Count every atom on the drawing, the groups above and below included.

steps.working: Repeat unit: the same 2 C, 2 H and 2 Cl, so $\ce{C2H2Cl2}$ again.
steps.decision: Only the bond between the carbons changed; no group was dropped or added.

steps.working: $M_r = 2 \times 12 + 2 \times 1 + 2 \times 35.5 = 97$ for both.
steps.decision: The same atoms give the same relative formula mass, using the Data Leaflet's values.

stem: Draw and name the monomer of the chain above. **[2]**

steps.working: Mark off two neighbouring carbons: one with F and H, one with H and H.
steps.decision: Each monomer brought two carbons into the chain, so the pattern repeats every two.

steps.working: Remove the two bonds that joined the unit to its neighbours.
steps.decision: Those bonds were made when the monomers linked, so they are the ones that go.

steps.working: Put the C=C back between the two carbons: $\ce{CH2=CHF}$.
steps.decision: The step most often missed: without the C=C it would be an alkane, which could never have polymerised.

steps.working: Two carbons, a C=C and one F: **fluoroethene**.
steps.decision: Name it as the alkene with its group, exactly as the monomer is named.

prompt: Working back from a section of polymer chain to its monomer, what is the last step?
options: put the C=C back between the two carbons of the unit
remove the bonds that join the unit to its neighbours
mark off two neighbouring carbons that repeat
answer: put the C=C back between the two carbons of the unit
explain: The order is mark off two carbons, remove the outer bonds, then put the double bond back: steps 1 to 3 of See it. The last step is the one most often left out, and without it the answer is an alkane, which could never have polymerised.

optionNotes.option: remove the bonds that join the unit to its neighbours
optionNotes.why: Removing the outer bonds comes second; stopping there leaves a molecule with no C=C, an alkane that could never have polymerised.

optionNotes.option: mark off two neighbouring carbons that repeat
optionNotes.why: Marking off the unit is where the method starts, not where it ends.

twin.prompt: Working back from a section of polymer chain to its monomer, what is the first step?
options: mark off two neighbouring carbons that repeat
put the C=C back between the two carbons
count every hydrogen in the chain
twin.answer: mark off two neighbouring carbons that repeat
twin.explain: Step 1 of See it: each monomer brought two carbons, so a unit is two neighbouring carbons. Only then are the outer bonds removed and the C=C put back.

optionNotes.option: put the C=C back between the two carbons
optionNotes.why: Putting the C=C back is the last step; first you need the two carbons it goes between.

optionNotes.option: count every hydrogen in the chain
optionNotes.why: The whole chain's hydrogens tell you nothing about one monomer; you count the atoms of one two-carbon unit.

prompt: A section of an addition polymer printed in a question shows eight carbon atoms in its chain. How many repeat units does it show?
options: four
eight
two
explain: Each monomer's C=C brought two carbons into the chain, as step 1 of See it marked off, so every two chain carbons are one repeat unit however long the printed section is. Eight chain carbons are four units.

optionNotes.option: eight
optionNotes.why: Eight counts the chain carbons, but each repeat unit holds two of them.

optionNotes.option: two
optionNotes.why: Two is the number of chain carbons in one unit, not the number of units in the section.

twin.prompt: A printed section of an addition polymer shows fourteen carbon atoms in its chain. How many monomer molecules joined to make that section?
options: seven
fourteen
two
twin.explain: Each monomer brought two chain carbons, so fourteen carbons came from seven monomer molecules, one for each repeat unit.

optionNotes.option: fourteen
optionNotes.why: Fourteen counts carbons, but each monomer brought two of them.

optionNotes.option: two
optionNotes.why: Two is the number of chain carbons one monomer brings, not the number of monomers.

md: A chain can carry a group bigger than one atom, such as $\ce{CH3}$. The method does not change: mark off two chain carbons, put the C=C back between them, and count the side groups' carbons too when you write the monomer's formula.

stem: Every second carbon of the chain above carries two $\ce{CH3}$ groups. Write the molecular formula of the monomer. **[1]**

steps.working: One unit: a $\ce{CH2}$ and a carbon carrying two $\ce{CH3}$ groups.
steps.decision: Two chain carbons, as always; the CH₃ groups hang off the second of them.

steps.working: Remove the outer bonds and put the C=C back: $\ce{CH2=C(CH3)2}$.
steps.decision: The side groups stay on the carbon they were on.

steps.working: Count: $2 + 2 = 4$ carbons and $2 + 6 = 8$ hydrogens, so $\ce{C4H8}$.
steps.decision: The side groups' carbons belong to the monomer; leaving them out is how this mark is lost.

prompt: In another addition polymer, every second carbon of the chain carries a Cl atom and a CH₃ group, and the others carry two H atoms. Give the molecular formula of the monomer.
answer: C3H5Cl | C₃H₅Cl | C3ClH5 | CH2=C(CH3)Cl | CH2=CClCH3 | CH2CClCH3 | CH2C(CH3)Cl | CH3CCl=CH2
explain: Put the C=C back into one two-carbon unit, as step 2 of See it did: $\ce{CH2=C(CH3)Cl}$. Then count every atom, the side group's included: 3 C, $2 + 3 = 5$ H and 1 Cl, so $\ce{C3H5Cl}$.

twin.prompt: Every second carbon of a chain carries a Cl atom and an F atom, and the others carry two H atoms. Give the molecular formula of the monomer.
twin.answer: C2H2ClF | C₂H₂ClF | C2H2FCl | CH2=CClF | CH2CClF | CH2=CFCl
twin.explain: One unit is a CH₂ and a carbon carrying Cl and F. Put the C=C back, CH₂=CClF, and count: 2 C, 2 H, 1 Cl and 1 F.

md: **A monomer you have never met** (2019, 2021). The paper draws an unfamiliar alkene, such as $\ce{CF2=CF2}$ or $\ce{CH2=CHBr}$, and asks for its polymer. The method does not change: open the C=C and copy every group.
**An old or trade name** (2019, 2021). PTFE or polyvinyl bromide may be named in the stem. Read the structure, not the name, and write poly(monomer) whenever a name is asked for.
**A long section of chain** (2022). However long the printed chain, a unit is two carbons, and each unit came from one monomer.
**Two names, two marks** (2022, 2025). The process is worth two marks, addition and polymerisation; the polymer's name is worth one.

stem: Chlorotrifluoroethene, $\ce{CF2=CFCl}$, is drawn above. Describe the repeat unit of its polymer. **[2]**

steps.working: The C=C opens to a single bond between the two carbons.
steps.decision: An unfamiliar monomer is handled exactly like ethene: one bond of the double bond opens.

steps.working: Copy every group: two F on the first carbon, an F and a Cl on the second.
steps.decision: Count them against the monomer: three F and one Cl, nothing lost.

steps.working: A bond through each bracket, and n after the closing bracket.
steps.decision: The same drawing marks as for any monomer.

prompt: Tetrafluoroethene, C₂F₄, has a C=C with two fluorine atoms on each carbon. What goes between the two carbons of its repeat unit?
options: a single bond, with two F on each carbon
a double bond, with two F on each carbon
a single bond, with one F on each carbon
answer: a single bond, with two F on each carbon
explain: The rule is the same for any monomer, as See it showed for chlorotrifluoroethene: one bond of the C=C opens, leaving a single bond, and every group stays where it was. Two F on each carbon in the monomer means two F on each carbon in the unit.

optionNotes.option: a double bond, with two F on each carbon
optionNotes.why: The groups are right, but keeping the double bond would give each carbon five bonds once the bonds through the brackets are drawn.

optionNotes.option: a single bond, with one F on each carbon
optionNotes.why: The bond is right, but two fluorines have gone missing, and no atom leaves when the monomers join.

twin.prompt: 1,1-Difluoroethene is CH₂=CF₂. What does the repeat unit of its polymer show on its two carbons?
options: two H on one carbon and two F on the other, joined by a single bond
one H and one F on each carbon, joined by a single bond
two H on one carbon and two F on the other, joined by a double bond
twin.answer: two H on one carbon and two F on the other, joined by a single bond
twin.explain: Open the C=C to a single bond and copy each carbon's own groups: the carbon that had two H keeps them, and the one that had two F keeps those.

optionNotes.option: one H and one F on each carbon, joined by a single bond
optionNotes.why: The atoms are all there, but they have been moved: each carbon keeps exactly the groups it had in the monomer.

optionNotes.option: two H on one carbon and two F on the other, joined by a double bond
optionNotes.why: The groups are right, but the double bond is the one thing that must open when the chain forms.

md: The hardest shape is a monomer with a group bigger than one atom on its C=C, such as methylpropene, $\ce{CH2=C(CH3)2}$. Only the **two carbons of the C=C** go into the chain; every other carbon hangs off it as a **side group**. Three or four carbons in a row inside the brackets loses the mark.

title: Where the specification stops
md: Condensation polymers, natural polymers and plastics recycling are not on the CCEA Double Award specification.

stem: Draw the repeat unit of the polymer made from methylpropene, $\ce{CH2=C(CH3)2}$. **[2]**

steps.working: The C=C joins carbon 1 and carbon 2: those two make the chain.
steps.decision: Find the double bond first: only its two carbons gain a spare bond.

steps.working: A single bond between them: H and H on the first, two $\ce{CH3}$ groups on the second.
steps.decision: Both CH₃ groups hang off the chain; neither joins the row.

steps.working: A bond through each bracket and n after the closing bracket; check: $\ce{C4H8}$, the monomer's atoms.
steps.decision: The atom count proves no side-group carbon was lost.

prompt: Hex-1-ene, CH₂=CHCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃, forms an addition polymer. How many carbon atoms of each repeat unit sit in the main chain, inside the brackets?
explain: Only the two carbons of the C=C join the chain, as step 1 of See it showed. The other four carbons make one side group hanging off the second chain carbon, so two are in the chain.

twin.prompt: How many carbon atoms are in the side group of each repeat unit of poly(hex-1-ene)?
twin.explain: Six carbons in the monomer and two in the chain: the other four make one side group, hanging off the second chain carbon.

md:
Name the process, **addition polymerisation**, and any polymer: poly(monomer).
Draw a repeat unit: a **single** C–C bond, a bond through each **bracket**, **n**; n on both sides of the equation.
Check it: the **same atoms** as the monomer, four bonds at every carbon.
Work back from a chain to its monomer by putting the **C=C** back.
Keep side groups off the chain, whatever the monomer.

Polymers sit inside the organic question of the C2 paper. The first marks are names: the process, or the polymer from its monomer. At Higher the last marks are a drawing: a repeat unit, a structural equation with n on both sides, or a monomer from a section of chain. Stuck? Draw the monomer, open its double bond, count four bonds at every carbon. The Sheet lists the traps.
